description: Hi! We're working on CrewPulse, an astronaut health monitoring concept for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We're interested in space exploration, healthcare technology, research, and product design. I contribute through 3D CAD modeling, research, and concept design. We're looking for teammates skilled in programming, UI/UX, data analysis, biomedical engineering, or space science. Most importantly, I value creativity, teamwork, and curiosity!
summary: CrewPulse is a health-monitoring web app for astronauts on long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars. On Mars, a message to Earth can take up to 22 minutes each way, so crews can’t count on a flight surgeon answering in real time. CrewPulse brings sensor readings, a two-minute daily check-in and symptom reports together in one place. It compares each reading with that astronaut’s own usual range and tells the crew, in plain language, how serious a problem is and what to do next. An interactive body map colours each area by severity and shows trends and self-care steps. The onboard medical officer and the ground flight surgeon each get their own view, and changes sent from Earth travel with the real communication delay. Our team also designed eight sensor devices in CAD, shown as interactive 3D models. CrewPulse matters because the further crews travel, the more they need to recognise and respond to health problems on their own.
details:
What it does. CrewPulse has three roles: crew member, onboard medical officer and ground flight surgeon. Guests can try it without an account.

  • Crew see an at-a-glance dashboard of heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, sleep, glucose and mood, each with a 14-day trend against their personal range.
  • The daily check-in and a free-text symptom checker combine symptoms with sensor readings. When several symptoms add up, the app escalates to “act now” and opens step-by-step action cards.
  • The body map colours 8 areas (head, eyes, neck, shoulders, chest, abdomen, arms, legs) by severity and explains what each finding means in space.
  • Medical staff see every crew member’s status at a glance. Alert limits changed from Earth arrive after the communication delay and need the medical officer’s confirmation.
  • An environment panel tracks cabin CO₂, radiation dose and space weather.

Benefits and impact. Crews can catch problems earlier and act before Earth can respond. The medical officer gets one clear view instead of scattered data, and ground teams stay informed despite the delay.

Creativity. Alerts are delay-aware and need medical-officer confirmation. Each astronaut is compared with their own baseline instead of population averages. A 3D hardware showcase lets judges spin our own CAD devices, including an orbital mass-measurement rig, because you can’t use a scale without gravity.

What we considered. We considered:

  • the communication delay
  • plain language a non-doctor can act on
  • honest labelling: every simulated reading is marked “Simulated”, and the hardware is hobby-grade, not flight-qualified
  • privacy, by giving each role only the data it needs
  • colourblind-safe status icons and labels
  • working on phones and laptops
  • working offline as a single file

Tools.

  • Website: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with SVG graphics and WebGL 3D.
  • CAD: Onshape, exported as STEP files.
  • Model conversion: a Python STEP-to-glTF converter (NumPy, SciPy).
  • Testing: Playwright.
  • Planned prototype parts: ESP32 microcontroller, AD8232/MAX86150 heart sensors, an IMU and temperature sensors.
  • AI assistance: Claude.
